text: You've decided fine-tuning is actually worth it for your use case. So what does that process actually look like, mechanically? This lesson walks it using OpenAI's fine-tuning API as the real, concrete example — the major self-serve flow still running today.

Four stages, whichever provider is running it. Prepare your training data as JSONL — one example conversation per line. Upload that file and create a job, referencing it and picking a base model. The job trains asynchronously, moving through a status from validating to running to succeeded, or failed. And once it succeeds, you call the result exactly like any other model.

Here's what one line of that training file actually looks like — the exact same messages shape from Lesson 13, a user turn and an assistant turn, just saved to a file instead of sent live. Your training file is just hundreds of these, one per line.

And here's the real request that kicks off training: a POST to fine_tuning slash jobs, with just a model and a training_file reference. Two fields, sane defaults. You can override hyperparameters like epochs or batch size, but the right starting move is almost always to leave them alone unless you have a specific, measured reason not to.

Once the job succeeds, you get back a fine_tuned_model field — a brand new model ID string. And here's the good news: you call it exactly like any other model, in the exact same chat completion shape from Lesson 13. Nothing about how you use it changes, only which model string you pass.

Prepare, upload, train, call — that's fine-tuning's real mechanical shape on the provider still running it self-serve. Worth remembering: the Claude path looks structurally different, running through Amazon Bedrock instead. Next lesson covers a technique that makes training itself dramatically cheaper: LoRA. See you there.
